style.summary:
style of A: A is quick and collaborative, with short confirmations and restarts that sound agreeable.
style of B: B is direct and matter-of-fact, stating what has already been done.

A: A's quick, collaborative tone keeps the exchange moving toward A's proposal.
A's restarts show A pushing to get the point across, which gives A the initiative.
A's agreeable confirmations make A's plan feel like the shared direction.
B: B's matter-of-fact tone gives B's facts the weight of settled information.
B's direct statements shape the register of the exchange toward B's view.
B's correction of A's reference shows B holding the reliable record.

A: A's quick tone is a style of speed, and B's facts decide what the plan rests on.
A's restarts show A losing the thread, which leaves B holding the initiative.
Agreeable confirmations only shape direction if B accepts them, so B controls the shared view.
B: B's directness is an assertion that A can contest at any point.
B's statements are only the register because A's proposal invites them.
Correcting a reference is a small point that does not establish B's authority over the plan.

content.summary:
content of A: A proposes doing the same thing again on the Meeting Recorder set.
content of B: B supplies the fact that non-natives were excluded earlier and sets the scope of recognition.

A: A proposes the plan to repeat the earlier approach, which sets the direction.
A's conclusion that the group should do the same thing becomes the outcome of the exchange.
A's proposal establishes the reference point the group works from.
B: B's fact about the earlier exclusion grounds the decision in what has already happened.
B's statement that recognition of non-natives is unnecessary defines the scope.
B's knowledge of what was done previously is the evidence the group relies on.

A: A's proposal depends on B's fact, so B's knowledge decides whether the plan holds.
A's conclusion only follows once B confirms the earlier exclusion, so B has the decisive say.
A's reference point is only valid if B's account of the past is correct.
B: B's fact is a supporting detail that A can use or ignore when setting the direction.
B's statement of scope is a proposal, and A's reply sets the direction.
B's correction is cut short by A's continued speech, so A controls the grounding.

coordination.summary:
coordination of A: A cuts in and completes the thought, taking the turn at key points.
coordination of B: B is interrupted and interrupts in turn, giving the historical fact in overlapping speech.

A: A cuts in to complete B's sentence, which gives A the last word on the point.
A's 'Yeah. So we want...' closes the exchange by stating the conclusion.
A takes the turn at the moment of decision, which gives A control of the transition.
B: B's interruptions show B holding the floor when the point matters.
B's correction shows B tracking the record and directing the discussion.
B's statement of scope comes first and frames what follows.

A: A's interruption shows A being cut off by B's speech, which weakens A's claim to the last word.
A's conclusion only holds because B confirmed the earlier exclusion, so B has the decisive say.
A's control of the transition depends on B pausing, so B decides when the turn passes.
B: B's interruptions are reactive and do not settle the outcome.
B's correction is a fact the group can take or leave.
B's statement of scope comes before A's proposal, but A's proposal sets what follows.

engagement.summary:
engagement of A: A draws on past work and proposes continuity, showing engagement with the plan.
engagement of B: B is focused on the technical point and supplies the justification.

A: A's proposal to continue past work shows A's commitment to the project.
A's push to finish the thought shows A is invested in the outcome.
A's reference to earlier work makes A the carrier of project history.
B: B's focus on the technical point shows deep engagement with the subject.
B's justification gives the group reasons to trust B's view.
B's knowledge of what was excluded makes B the expert in the discussion.

A: Proposing continuity depends on B accepting the past work, so B holds that decision.
Pushing to finish a thought is a form of pressure that B can ignore.
Carrying history is valuable only if B confirms that history is accurate.
B: Focus on a technical point is narrow and does not establish B's control of the plan.
Justification is only persuasive if A accepts it, so A makes the final call.
Expertise on exclusions is a fact A can draw on without giving B the decision.
